newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican lawman began with bang, ended in whimper.
newsitem.headline: Mexican lawman began with bang, ended in whimper.

text.p: Conservative lawyer Antonio Lozano Gracia, who was fired as Mexico's attorney general on Monday, came into office as a new broom in one of the country's most corrupt institutions but left two years later trailing accusations of incompetence.
The only opposition politician ever to serve in a Mexican Cabinet, Lozano, 43, started with a bang.

Within weeks of taking up his post in December 1994 he fired 513 corrupt cops. Three months later he broke unprecedented ground by ordering the arrest of ex-president Carlos Salinas de Gortari's brother Raul on murder charges.
That broke an old taboo in Mexico that protected former presidents and their families from the reach of the law.
The following year Lozano scored another first by arresting cocaine cartel chief Juan Garcia Abrego and putting him on a plane to the United States for trial.
Washington was thrilled -- but Mexicans asked why Lozano's team were not able to try and imprison him at home.

As time wore on, more questions were asked about the failure of Lozano's office to assemble strong evidence against Raul Salinas in the September 1994 murder of ruling party secretary-general Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu or in a parallel illicit enrichment case.

But the final faux pas came when Lozano had investigators dig up in October a skeleton in the grounds of a ranch near Mexico City used by Raul Salinas -- tipping off reporters beforehand to expect a big breakthrough.

Lozano publicly predicted the remains would turn out to be those of Manuel Munoz Rocha, a missing legislator whom prosecutors believed Raul Salinas had used to arrange the murder, then killed -- but he then failed to prove it.
Raul's lawyers accused Lozano of planting the body and ridiculed detectives for relying on the evidence of a clairvoyant to locate the body.

In the other high-profile murder case in which Lozano promised much but failed to deliver, prosecutors' efforts to prove a conspiracy lay behind the March 23, 1994 assassination of ruling party presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio also fell apart as suspects were freed for lack of evidence.
Previously a congressman for the National Action Party (PAN), Lozano shrugged off the criticism and pressed on with efforts to clean up the notoriously venal police.
In August he fired another 700 members of the Federal Judicial Police, the country's most powerful. But even that went wrong: many of them won court orders allowing them to get their jobs back.
